title: Communicable Disease Terminology
body:
## What it is
These are the vocabulary words that the board exam uses to separate look-alike ideas. Most questions are not "define X" but "which one of these two words fits this situation". Learn the pairs and the contrasts, because a wrong word in a stem or option is usually the neighbour of the right one: infection vs disease, carrier vs case, isolation vs quarantine, concurrent vs terminal disinfection, endemic vs epidemic.

## Key points
**Infection and disease**
- **Infection**: an organism lodges and multiplies in host tissue and may cause signs, symptoms and an immune response. Infection is not always disease: a person can be infected and feel well.
- **Communicable disease**: an illness caused by an infectious agent or its toxins that passes, directly or indirectly (through a vector, vehicle or object), from an infected source to a susceptible person. **Contagious** means it spreads easily from person to person.
- **Zoonosis**: an infectious disease that passes from a non-human animal to humans (WHO uses this meaning; rabies is the classic example) [2,3].
- **Infectious disease** in the old handout is used in a narrower way: spread that needs direct inoculation through broken skin or mucous membrane rather than casual contact. Many textbooks use "infectious" and "communicable" more loosely, so read the stem carefully.

**People in the picture**
- **Case**: a person who has the disease. A **carrier** harbors the organism and can pass it on without showing disease. Carriers are hard to find, so they are an important hidden source of spread. The CDC chain-of-infection page makes the same point: carriers often do not know they are infected [2].
- **Contact**: any person or animal that has been closely associated with an infected person or with freshly soiled material, so that infection was possible.
- **Host**: the person, animal or plant on which a parasite depends. **Susceptible host**: a person without enough immunity to resist the agent.
- **Reservoir**: the place where the agent normally lives and multiplies (humans, animals or the environment such as soil or water). The reservoir is not always the direct source of infection [2]. **Habitat** is where an organism normally lives.
- **Vector**: a living carrier (such as a mosquito) that moves the agent from one host to another. **Vehicle**: a non-living carrier such as food, water, blood or an object.

**Levels of disease occurrence (CDC wording)** [1]
- **Sporadic**: occurs infrequently and irregularly.
- **Endemic**: the constant, usual presence of a disease in a population within a geographic area; the baseline or expected level.
- **Hyperendemic**: persistent, high levels of occurrence.
- **Epidemic**: a sudden or gradual rise in cases above what is normally expected in that population and area. **Outbreak** has the same meaning but is often used for a smaller geographic area.
- **Pandemic**: an epidemic that has spread across several countries or continents, usually affecting many people.

**Cleaning and separating**
- **Disinfection**: destroying pathogens on inanimate objects by physical or chemical means.
  - **Concurrent disinfection**: done right after the client discharges infectious material, while the client is still a source of infection (for example disposing of soiled dressings and cleaning excreta at once).
  - **Terminal disinfection**: done when the client is no longer a source, for example after discharge or transfer, to prepare the room for the next client.
- **Isolation**: separating a sick (infectious) person from others during the period of communicability.
- **Quarantine**: limiting the movement of *exposed but not necessarily sick* people or animals for a period equal to the longest incubation period of that disease.
- **Incubation period**: time from exposure to first symptoms. **Period of communicability**: time during which the person can pass the agent on, which may begin before symptoms.

## Nursing application
- Use the right word when you document and report: a *suspected case* is reported even before confirmation; a *contact* is traced and counseled; a *carrier* is educated about hygiene and may be restricted from food handling.
- For an isolated client the nurse applies the precautions ordered or chosen for the transmission route (see [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]) and explains why to the family.
- For exposed but well people (quarantine or monitoring), the nurse teaches symptom watching for the length of the incubation period, whom to call, and how to avoid exposing others.
- After a client who was a source leaves, make sure terminal cleaning is arranged; during the stay, handle discharges, dressings and linens with concurrent disinfection.
- Doctors diagnose and order treatment; the nurse observes, reports, teaches, implements infection-control measures and carries out ordered therapy.

## Philippine context
Communicable diseases are reportable to the local health unit; the Philippine reporting and sanitation laws are summarized in [[Philippine Laws on Disease Reporting, Immunization, Sanitation and Environment]]. Several diseases are endemic in specific Philippine areas (see [[Locally Endemic Diseases]]). UNVERIFIED: the exact reporting rules and time limits should be checked in the DOH issuance in force.

## Exam traps
- **Isolation = the sick person; quarantine = the exposed person.** This pair is a favorite.
- **Concurrent vs terminal**: ask whether the client is still the source. Still a source = concurrent; no longer a source = terminal.
- **Endemic does not mean mild or rare.** A high but constant, expected level is still endemic (or hyperendemic); only a rise above the expected level is an epidemic.
- **Carrier vs case**: a carrier has no disease; do not call a carrier "sick".
- **Contagious vs communicable**: all contagious diseases are communicable, but not every communicable disease (for example one spread only by vector) is contagious person to person.
- **Reservoir vs vector**: the reservoir is where the agent lives; the vector is the carrier that moves it.

## Quick memory aids
- **I**solation = **I**ll people; **Q**uarantine = **Q**uestionable (exposed, might be sick).
- Concurrent = "while still running" (client is a source); terminal = "the end of the stay".
- Sporadic = scattered, endemic = expected, epidemic = excess, pandemic = planet-wide.

## Related topics
[[Chain of Infection and Modes of Transmission]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]], [[Epidemiologic Triangle and Patterns of Disease Occurrence]], [[Types of Immunity and Antigens]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]]

## References
1. CDC archive, Principles of Epidemiology Lesson 1 Section 11 (patterns of disease): https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section11.html
2. CDC archive, Principles of Epidemiology Lesson 1 Section 10 (chain of infection): https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section10.html
3. WHO, Zoonoses fact sheet: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/zoonoses
4. CDC, Guideline for Isolation Precautions (2007, last update 2024): https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/media/pdfs/Guideline-Isolation-H.pdf

## Check against your textbook

UNVERIFIED: definitions of concurrent and terminal disinfection were not found on a fetched page; they are kept from the handout.
