Treat this as a dated statement; check the DOH for the current status.
- The Department of Agriculture Bureau of Animal Industry leads culling, 1 km quarantine zones and surveillance in poultry (news summary), working with LGUs and the DOH.
- DOH emphasizes border control for travelers and imported poultry products, and readiness of health and animal sectors.
- RA 11332 (2019) requires immediate reporting of notifiable diseases and health events by public and private entities, including avian influenza if on the list (UNVERIFIED on fetched pages).
- Local exam angle: a poultry worker or backyard chicken raiser with flu-like illness after chickens died suddenly.

## Exam traps
- Nurse vs doctor: the nurse isolates, assesses and reports; the physician orders testing and oseltamivir; animal culling is done by agriculture authorities, not nurses.
- Priority trap: airway and breathing and strict isolation come before teaching or specimen collection; ask about poultry exposure.
- Safety trap: rapid flu tests are unreliable for novel influenza A; do not rule out bird flu on a negative rapid test.
- Properly cooked poultry and eggs are not a source of infection.
- Do not delay oseltamivir while waiting for lab results.

## Quick memory aids
- "Bird flu = bird + flu + breathing trouble: ask about birds."
- PPE set for suspected novel flu: standard, contact, airborne plus eyes.
- "Cook it, wash it, report it."

## References
1. WHO. Influenza (avian and other zoonotic) fact sheet: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/influenza-(avian-and-other-zoonotic)
2. CDC. Clinicians evaluating patients for avian influenza: https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/hcp/clinicians-evaluating-patients/index.html
3. CDC. Bird flu situation summary: https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/situation-summary/index.html
4. GMA News. DOH says no confirmed human case of avian influenza yet in PH (Jan 2023): http://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/857341/doh-says-no-confirmed-human-case-of-avian-influenza-yet-in-ph/story

## Check against your textbook
The handout is brief: add the viral subtype, treatment, and the current DOH reporting rules.
UNVERIFIED: the 3-5 day human incubation from the handout, the handout's farm control measures as a nursing duty, and the current human case status in the Philippines.

title: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS)
body:
## What it is
Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) is a viral respiratory disease caused by the SARS coronavirus (SARS-CoV-1). Cases were first detected in Guangdong, China in November 2002 and the illness spread to 28 other countries (WHO). The handout dates worldwide surveillance from 12 March 2003 and the first Philippine case on 11 April 2003; a CDC alert from 2003 lists the Philippines among the places reporting suspect cases. The WHO source gives a case fatality of about 9.6 percent. It is the handout's example of an epidemic spread by air travel and in health care settings, so it tests isolation, PPE and the first action on a suspected case.

## Causative agent
- Organism: SARS-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV), family Coronaviridae, an RNA virus. Bats of the genus *Rhinolophus* carry related viruses.
- Mode of transmission: Close person-to-person contact; mainly respiratory droplets from coughing and sneezing, touching contaminated surfaces then the mouth, nose or eyes, and spread through small particles in the air, which WHO describes. Airborne spread was possible but not fully understood (Iowa HHS). It spread within households and in health care settings.
- Incubation period: usually 2 to 7 days, sometimes up to 10 days (WHO); the handout gives a mean of 5 days, range 2 to 10, up to 14; another source gives 3 to 10 days and rarely up to 14.
- Period of communicability: clients are most contagious when symptomatic, especially in the second week of illness, with a maximum of less than 21 days (Iowa HHS).
- Reservoir: bats of the genus *Rhinolophus* carry related viruses; humans spread it. UNVERIFIED: any current Philippine reservoir or vector.

## Main problem
The virus infects the lower respiratory tract and causes diffuse alveolar damage and inflammation. Oxygen exchange falls, leading to hypoxia and acute respiratory distress. Some clients need mechanical ventilation (10 to 20 percent per WHO). The main problems are airway and breathing, and containing spread.

## Initial manifestations
- Prodromal phase: sudden high fever above 38 C (the first sign), chills, malaise, headache and muscle pain.
- Dry non-productive cough or shortness of breath that follows 3 to 7 days after the fever.
- Screening cues: travel to an affected area or close contact with a suspected or probable case within 10 days.

## Other manifestations
- Respiratory phase: hypoxia, crackles, dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds, with or without respiratory distress; most clients develop pneumonia.
- Diarrhea, loss of appetite and fatigue in some.
- Complications: acute respiratory distress syndrome, respiratory failure, death; most patients were previously healthy adults aged 25 to 70.

## Laboratory and diagnostic data
- Chest X-ray: patchy infiltrates or pneumonia.
- Blood tests: low lymphocyte count and low oxygen saturation or abnormal blood gas. UNVERIFIED: exact lab pattern not in the pages fetched.
- Specific confirmation is by laboratory testing for the virus (antibody or nucleic acid tests); collection is guided by the public health laboratory. UNVERIFIED.

## Medical management
- The physician applies the case definition (fever, respiratory symptoms, travel or contact), isolates suspected cases and orders the tests.
- No specific treatment existed when SARS emerged; care is supportive (oxygen, ventilation, fluids). WHO notes that antivirals and vaccines developed in COVID-19 research may help against SARS-CoV-1.
- The physician reports to public health authorities and manages complications such as respiratory failure.
- Outbreak control relies on surveillance, isolation, contact tracing, 10-day quarantine of contacts and exit screening (WHO).

## Pharmacologic care
- Oxygen: a drug; give the ordered flow and route. Before: assess saturation and breathing effort. During: keep the mask or cannula in place, watch for hypoxia and distress. After: record the response and report falling saturation.
- Antipyretics (prototype paracetamol): lower fever and relieve aches. Dose per physician order. Check temperature before and after; report fever that does not fall.
- Antivirals, steroids and antibiotics: used only on the physician's order for specific problems (antibiotics treat added bacterial infection, not the virus). Dose per physician order; check allergy and watch for adverse effects. UNVERIFIED which agents are currently recommended.

## Nursing diagnoses
1. Impaired gas exchange related to alveolar inflammation as evidenced by hypoxia, dyspnea and crackles (priority).
2. Hyperthermia related to viral infection as evidenced by fever above 38 C and chills.
3. Risk for infection transmission related to respiratory spread of the virus.
4. Anxiety related to isolation and fear of death.

## Independent nursing interventions
1. Assess airway, respiratory rate, effort and saturation continuously - breathing comes first.
2. Position in semi-Fowler's to ease breathing; encourage deep breathing - improves lung expansion.
3. Isolate suspected and probable cases in a single room and use the precautions required by policy (standard, contact and droplet at minimum; airborne for aerosol-producing procedures). UNVERIFIED: the exact precaution set was not stated in the pages fetched. Put a mask on the client during transport - limits spread.
4. Use full PPE (gown, gloves, eye protection, respirator or mask per policy) and strict handwashing - health workers were often infected.
5. Screen visitors and the client for travel history and contact - finds more cases.
6. Provide fluids, rest and fever comfort; explain isolation and give emotional support - reduces anxiety.
7. Report suspected cases at once to the infection control officer and health authorities - starts contact tracing.

## Collaborative nursing interventions
1. As ordered: Give oxygen - check saturation, set the flow, and report worsening distress or falling saturation.
2. As ordered: Give antipyretics - check temperature before and after and do not exceed the order.
3. As ordered: Collect throat swab, blood or sputum samples with full PPE - label and send as the laboratory instructs.
4. As ordered: Assist with intubation, ventilation or chest X-ray - use airborne PPE during aerosol-producing procedures.
5. As ordered: Give IV fluids - monitor intake and output and lung sounds for overload.

## Philippine context
- The DOH surveillance and response system tracks epidemic-prone diseases; RA 11332 (2019) requires immediate, accurate reporting of notifiable diseases and health events of public health concern. Whether SARS is on the current list was not verified.
- Port health and airport screening apply to suspected travelers (WHO notes exit screening). UNVERIFIED for local procedures.
- Local trap: the first action for a traveler with fever and cough is isolation and screening, not discharge or teaching about hygiene.

## Exam traps
- **Priority trap (ABC):** A client with SARS-like illness who becomes cyanotic and dyspneic: support airway, breathing and oxygen before completing the travel history.
- **Nurse vs doctor trap:** The nurse isolates, applies PPE, reports and assesses; the physician applies the case definition and orders tests and drugs.
- **Fever trap:** Fever above 38 C plus travel or contact is the key clue.
- **Precaution trap:** Do not choose only handwashing; choose isolation and PPE.

## Quick memory aids
- **SARS = Spread by air and sneezes; Self-protect first.**
- Fever first, **cough 3 to 7 days later**.
- Report, isolate, protect: **R-I-P**.

## References
1. World Health Organization. Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS). https://www.who.int/health-topics/severe-acute-respiratory-syndrome
2. Iowa Department of Health and Human Services. SARS. https://hhs.iowa.gov/health-prevention/providers-professionals/center-acute-disease-epidemiology/epi-manual/reportable-diseases/sars
3. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Health Alert Network notice on severe acute respiratory syndrome (2003, retired). https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/25031
4. Republic Act No. 11332 (2019), LawPhil. https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2019/ra_11332_2019.html

## Check against your textbook
The handout says "droplet contact"; confirm the precaution level (airborne and contact for aerosol-producing procedures). UNVERIFIED: exact precaution set, laboratory findings, specific drugs, the Philippine first-case date of 11 April 2003 (not seen in any fetched page) and whether SARS is notifiable under RA 11332. No textbook was read for this note.
See also [[Influenza]], [[Bird Flu (Avian Influenza)]], [[Epidemiologic Triangle and Patterns of Disease Occurrence]].

title: Cholera
body:
## What it is
Cholera is an acute intestinal infection caused by the bacterium *Vibrio cholerae*. It can range from no symptoms at all to sudden, massive, painless watery diarrhea with vomiting that drains the body of water and salts within hours. Left untreated, the patient slides into hypovolemic shock, metabolic acidosis and death. The germ is not the killer here; the fluid loss is. That one idea decides almost every nursing priority and every exam question on cholera.

## Causative agent
- Organism: *Vibrio cholerae*, a curved gram-negative rod. Only serogroups O1 and O139 cause outbreaks; O1 (the El Tor biotype in your handout) has caused recent outbreaks. It makes a toxin that forces the intestinal lining to pour out water.
- Transmission: fecal-oral. A person swallows food or water contaminated with the feces (or vomitus, per the handout) of a patient or carrier. Raw or undercooked shellfish from coastal or brackish water can also carry the germ. Casual person-to-person contact is an unlikely route.
- Incubation period: WHO gives 12 hours to 5 days. Your handout's 6-48 hours falls inside this range but is narrower; know both.
- Period of communicability: most infected people have no symptoms yet still shed bacteria in feces for about 1-10 days (WHO). The handout says patients stay infective during diarrhea and up to about 7 days after.
- Reservoir in the Philippines: humans (patients and symptom-free carriers) and contaminated water; the germ also lives in brackish and coastal water. Outbreaks follow floods, typhoons, crowded evacuation centers and unsafe water.

## Main problem
The cholera toxin makes the small-bowel lining secrete huge amounts of isotonic fluid. The patient loses water, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate faster than they can be replaced by drinking. The result is severe dehydration, hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis (hence deep rapid breathing) and shock, with kidney injury if shock is prolonged.

## Initial manifestations
- Sudden watery diarrhea, often pale and cloudy with flecks of mucus: the classic **rice-water stool**, usually without cramps or fever.
- Vomiting and nausea.
- Thirst, dry mouth, leg cramps (potassium and fluid loss).
- Most cases are mild or moderate; about 1 in 10 become severe.

## Other manifestations
- Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, dry skin and tongue, loss of skin turgor, "washerwoman's hands" (wrinkled fingertips), sunken fontanelle in infants, low urine output, rapid weak pulse, low blood pressure.
- Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul-type, from acidosis).
- Restlessness, lethargy, then unconsciousness in severe cases.
- Complications: hypovolemic shock, acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia (especially in children), electrolyte imbalance.

## Laboratory and diagnostic data
- Stool culture is the standard confirmation; a PCR test on stool can also detect *V. cholerae* (MedlinePlus). Rapid diagnostic tests are used in outbreaks for early detection (WHO).
- Rectal swab in a transport medium when stool is not available; handout also lists darkfield microscopy of stool.
- Blood chemistry: raised BUN and creatinine in dehydration; electrolytes and bicarbonate to guide replacement.
- Report suspected cases at once; confirmation should not delay treatment.

## Medical management
- The physician decides the degree of dehydration and orders the route of rehydration: oral rehydration solution for mild-to-moderate cases, rapid intravenous fluid for severe dehydration or shock (WHO).
- The physician orders an antibiotic for severe cases, based on local susceptibility. Antibiotics shorten illness but do not replace fluids. WHO does not recommend mass antibiotic prophylaxis.
- The physician orders laboratory work (culture, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine) and corrects potassium or acidosis if present.
- The physician (with public health staff) may decide on oral cholera vaccine campaigns in outbreak areas; WHO lists three prequalified oral vaccines.

## Pharmacologic care
- **Oral rehydration salts (ORS/ORESOL)**: replace water, sodium, glucose and potassium. Before: assess dehydration level and ability to drink. During: give small frequent sips, using clean water for mixing; if the patient vomits, wait 10 minutes and resume slowly. After: record intake, output and stools. Hold and report: persistent vomiting, no urine, worsening drowsiness. Teaching: mix the packet exactly as the label directs and discard leftovers after 24 hours (UNVERIFIED in fetched pages; verify against ORESOL packet label). Amount per physician order.
- **IV isotonic crystalloids** (for example Lactated Ringer's, 0.9% sodium chloride): rapid volume replacement in severe dehydration. Before: confirm order, check patency of two IV sites if possible. During: monitor vital signs and urine output; listen to lung bases. After: record intake/output. Hold and report: crackles, shortness of breath, swelling, no urine. Rate and volume per physician order.
- **Antibiotics**: given to severe cases to shorten the illness. Prototype names commonly used for cholera include doxycycline and azithromycin (UNVERIFIED: not named on the pages I fetched; your handout names tetracycline, chloramphenicol and furazolidone). Before: ask about allergies and pregnancy; check susceptibility results. During: give with water, on schedule. Adverse effects: nausea, rash, and tooth staining or photosensitivity with tetracyclines. Hold and report: rash, difficulty breathing, severe vomiting. Teaching: finish the course. Dose per physician order.
- **Zinc supplementation for children** with diarrhea is mentioned by CDC; dose per physician order.

## Nursing diagnoses
1. Deficient fluid volume related to profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting as evidenced by sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, rapid weak pulse and low urine output (priority).
2. Diarrhea related to intestinal toxin action as evidenced by frequent rice-water stools.
3. Risk for impaired skin integrity related to frequent stools and dehydration.
4. Risk for infection transmission related to fecal contamination.
5. Deficient knowledge of family regarding safe water and sanitation as evidenced by unsafe excreta disposal.

## Independent nursing interventions
1. Assess airway, breathing and circulation first; check vital signs, level of consciousness and signs of shock - shock kills first, so detect it early.
2. Assess hydration status (skin turgor, mucous membranes, eyes, fontanelle, thirst, urine) - this tells how urgent replacement is.
3. Keep an accurate record of intake, output, stool count and vomiting - guides replacement and shows trends.
4. Encourage oral fluids in small, frequent sips if the patient is awake and able to swallow - maintains hydration without waiting for an order.
5. Apply enteric precautions: handwashing before and after care, gloves with excreta, separate or labeled commode - prevents spread to other patients and staff.
6. Dispose of stool, vomitus and soiled linen safely; disinfect surfaces and use proper toilet or latrine - removes the source of infection.
7. Weigh daily and keep the patient warm and comfortable - weight reflects fluid status; chilling worsens shock.
8. Provide perianal skin care and oral hygiene - frequent stools break down skin.
9. Teach family to wash hands with soap, boil or chlorinate drinking water, cook food well and avoid raw shellfish - breaks the fecal-oral chain.
10. Report the case to the barangay or municipal health office and trace others with symptoms - cholera is a reportable disease.

## Collaborative nursing interventions
1. As ordered: start and regulate IV fluid for severe dehydration - verify the fluid and rate, watch the pulse, BP and urine output, and report crackles or breathlessness.
2. As ordered: give ORS - check the patient can swallow, give small frequent sips, and report vomiting that prevents intake.
3. As ordered: give the antibiotic - check allergies and culture results first, give on time, and report rash or severe vomiting.
4. As ordered: collect stool or rectal swab and send blood for electrolytes, BUN and creatinine - label correctly, use clean technique and send promptly.
5. As ordered: give potassium replacement or correct acidosis - verify the order with a second nurse, give only if urine is flowing, and report weakness or irregular heartbeat.
6. As ordered: give zinc to a child with diarrhea - confirm the order and age, and observe for vomiting.

## Philippine context
- DOH runs a Food and Waterborne Diseases Prevention and Control program and cholera is among the diseases under PIDSR (Philippine Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response); suspected cases are reported, investigated and laboratory-confirmed. UNVERIFIED: law numbers and the exact program name were not confirmed from a fetched page.
- Large outbreaks have followed typhoons and floods; evacuation centers need safe water, toilets and handwashing.
- Common local advice: boil water, chlorinate, wash hands, safe toilets (sanitary latrines), and give ORS (ORESOL) early for any diarrhea.
- Useful terms: *pagtatae* (diarrhea), *oresol* (ORS), *kubeta/palikuran* (toilet).

## Exam traps
- **Fluid first, not the germ.** If the question asks the priority action for a patient with rice-water stool and low BP, choose rehydration (ABCs and circulation), not isolation, antibiotic or specimen collection.
- **Nurse action vs doctor action:** Ordering IV fluid volume, antibiotic choice and the diagnosis of cholera are medical; the nurse independently assesses hydration, records intake/output, applies enteric precautions and encourages oral fluids.
- **Isolation type:** cholera needs enteric precautions (stool/vomitus), not airborne or droplet.
- **Antidiarrheals** are not the answer; replace fluids instead.
- Washerwoman's hands means dehydration, not a skin disease.

## Quick memory aids
- **Rice-water + thirst + shock = fluids**. Think "replace, replace, replace".
- **ORS first, IV if severe** - mild/moderate mouths, severe veins.
- "Cholera = Choke on water that is dirty": reminds the water-and-food route.

## References
1. World Health Organization. Cholera fact sheet. https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/cholera
2. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Cholera. https://www.cdc.gov/cholera/about/index.html
3. MedlinePlus. Cholera. https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000303.htm

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists chloramphenicol and furazolidone; current choices differ, and rehydration remains the mainstay.
UNVERIFIED: the named antibiotics (doxycycline, azithromycin) and the ORS preparation details are not stated on the pages I fetched.
UNVERIFIED: the handout's incubation (6-48 hours) is narrower than WHO's 12 hours to 5 days.
UNVERIFIED: PIDSR details and any Philippine law number for reporting were not confirmed from a fetched page.
See also [[Typhoid Fever]], [[Bacillary Dysentery (Shigellosis)]], [[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]].

title: Typhoid Fever
body:
## What it is
An acute, systemic bacterial infection caused by *Salmonella typhi*, characterized by prolonged fever, sustained bacteremia, and bacterial localization in the reticuloendothelial system (lymph nodes, liver, spleen, Peyer's patches of the intestine). Other names: enteric fever, slow fever.

## Causative agent
*Salmonella typhi* (a Gram-negative, flagellated, facultative anaerobic bacillus). Transmission is strictly fecal-oral via contaminated food and water, ingestion of raw shellfish from polluted waters, or handling by asymptomatic chronic carriers (e.g., 'Typhoid Mary'). Incubation period is typically 6 to 30 days (CDC). Period of communicability persists as long as bacilli are excreted in excreta (from a week through convalescence; 2-5% become chronic carriers shedding via stool or urine).

## Main problem
Ingested bacilli invade the mucosal epithelium of the small intestine, pass into the lymphatic system and bloodstream (bacteremia), and multiply within macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. They subsequently localize in the lymphoid tissue of the terminal ileum (Peyer's patches), leading to hyperplasia, necrosis, severe ulceration, and high risk of intestinal hemorrhage or perforation during the third week of illness.

## Initial manifestations
- Insidious onset of sustained, step-ladder fever (gradually rising each day, peaking at 39°C to 40°C).
- Severe, dull frontal headache, malaise, generalized body weakness, and anorexia.
- Relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation: a slow heart rate relative to a high fever; a handout feature, not stated on the CDC pages fetched).
- Gastrointestinal disturbances: initially constipation in adults (or diarrhea in children), abdominal discomfort, and a coated tongue.

## Other manifestations
- Rose spots: faint, blanching, rose-colored maculopapular rashes appearing on the lower chest and abdomen during the 7th to 10th day (seen in about 30% of light-skinned patients).
- Splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and abdominal distension with tenderness in the right lower quadrant.
- Severe complications in the 3rd week: intestinal hemorrhage (melena) and intestinal perforation (sudden, sharp, agonizing right lower quadrant abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, board-like rigidity, and signs of peritonitis/shock).
- Neuropsychiatric symptoms ('typhoid state'): apathy, delirium, confusion, muttering delirium, and coma in severe untreated cases.

## Laboratory and diagnostic data
- Blood culture: the mainstay of diagnosis (CDC); most often positive in the first week of illness.
- Stool culture: positive from the second week onwards.
- Urine culture: positive from the second to third week.
- Widal test: an older antibody (agglutination) test that CDC does not recommend because of its high false-positive rate; it does not confirm the diagnosis. Some Philippine handouts still list it, so know it for recognition only.
- Complete blood count (CBC): typically shows leukopenia (low white blood cell count with relative neutropenia), unlike most bacterial infections which cause leukocytosis.

## Medical management
- Antibiotic therapy to eradicate the systemic infection, shorten the clinical course, and prevent relapses and carrier state.
- Supportive therapy: aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement for dehydration from fever and diarrhea.
- Surgical intervention: immediate exploratory laparotomy and surgical repair for intestinal perforation.

## Pharmacologic care
- Antibiotic Classes:
  - Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin, Ofloxacin): CDC advises NOT using fluoroquinolones for empiric treatment, because many strains are not susceptible; use only if the culture shows susceptibility. What they do: inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase.
  - Cephalosporins (e.g., Ceftriaxone IV): CDC lists ceftriaxone as an appropriate empiric option (resistance is common in travelers returning from Iraq and Pakistan).
  - Macrolides (e.g., Azithromycin): CDC lists azithromycin as an appropriate empiric option for uncomplicated illness. Aminopenicillins (e.g., Ampicillin/Amoxicillin): handout alternative, only by susceptibility result.
- Nurse's Responsibilities:
  - Before: Assess for drug allergies (especially penicillin/cephalosporin), review baseline liver and renal function tests, and check culture and sensitivity results.
  - During: Administer IV antimicrobials slowly as ordered; monitor infusion site for phlebitis; observe for signs of hypersensitivity reactions or superinfections (e.g., oral candidiasis, severe diarrhea).
  - After: Monitor temperature trends and clinical improvement; ensure the full course of antibiotics is completed even if fever subsides.
- Adverse effects and toxicity: Gastrointestinal upset, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, hepatotoxicity, and tendon rupture (fluoroquinolones).
- When to hold and report: Hold antibiotics and notify the physician immediately if signs of anaphylaxis, severe rash, severe watery diarrhea (Clostridioides difficile), or sudden drop in urine output occur.
- Health teaching: Emphasize complete adherence to the medication regimen; advise avoiding antacids containing aluminum or magnesium concurrently with quinolones (decreases absorption).

## Nursing diagnoses
1. Hyperthermia related to systemic inflammatory response to *Salmonella typhi* infection as evidenced by temperature of 39.5°C, flushed skin, and warm to touch. (priority)
2. Imbalanced Nutrition: Less Than Body Requirements related to hypermetabolic state, anorexia, and gastrointestinal ulceration as evidenced by weight loss and poor oral intake.
3. Acute Pain related to severe headache and abdominal distension as evidenced by verbalization of pain and guarding behavior.
4. Risk for Deficient Fluid Volume related to prolonged fever, vomiting, and potential gastrointestinal fluid losses.

## Independent nursing interventions
1. Monitor and record vital signs every 4 hours, paying close attention to temperature patterns and noting any pulse-temperature dissociation (relative bradycardia).
2. Implement non-pharmacological cooling measures (e.g., tepid sponge baths, applying a cool damp cloth to the forehead, maintaining a comfortable ambient room temperature, and lightweight clothing) to manage fever safely.
3. Administer frequent, small, soft, low-fiber, non-irritating, and easily digestible meals (e.g., soft diet, broths) as tolerated to prevent mechanical irritation of ulcerated Peyer's patches while maintaining nutritional support.
4. Monitor and record intake and output accurately; encourage frequent oral rehydration fluids (e.g., water, oresol, fruit juices) to replace insensible and GI fluid losses.
5. Enforce strict enteric precautions and standard precautions (meticulous hand hygiene with soap and water before and after patient contact, wearing gloves when handling body wastes, feces, or soiled linens) to prevent fecal-oral transmission.
6. Instruct the patient and family on proper personal hygiene, thorough handwashing after toilet use, safe food handling, drinking only boiled or potable water, and avoiding raw vegetables or street-vended foods.

## Collaborative nursing interventions
1. As ordered, administer prescribed antipyretics (e.g., Paracetamol) for high fever and discomfort; monitor temperature response and avoid aspirin in pediatric clients due to Reye's syndrome risk.
2. As ordered, administer intravenous fluids and electrolyte replacements; monitor IV infusion rates closely (especially in clients with cardiac or renal compromise) to prevent fluid overload.
3. As ordered, administer systemic antibiotic therapy (e.g., Ceftriaxone IV or Azithromycin PO, chosen by culture and susceptibility); monitor for therapeutic efficacy, therapeutic blood levels, and adverse reactions.
4. As ordered, collect diagnostic specimens (blood cultures first, then stool and urine cultures) using sterile technique and transport them promptly to the laboratory.
5. As ordered, maintain strict nothing-by-mouth (NPO) status and prepare the client for emergency surgical intervention if signs of intestinal perforation (sudden severe abdominal pain, board-like rigidity) occur.

## Philippine context
- Managed under the Department of Health (DOH) Philippine Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (PIDSR) framework.
- Strongly associated with community outbreaks during rainy seasons or when municipal water systems and sanitation facilities are compromised.
- Local exam traps: Confusing the constipation of typhoid with the watery/rice-water diarrhea of cholera; recognizing relative bradycardia (fever with a normal or slow heart rate);
identifying rose spots on the abdomen.

## Quick memory aids
- **TYPHOID**: **T**hree-week fever pattern; **Y**ellow-coated tongue; **P**ulse-temperature dissociation (relative bradycardia); **H**emorrhage/perforation risk in week 3; **O**ral/fecal route; **I**leum (Peyer's patches) ulceration; **D**iagnostic blood culture in week 1.

## Exam traps
- **Nurse vs. Doctor Trap**: The nurse assesses bowel sounds, abdominal rigidity, and vital signs, and reports sudden abdominal pain immediately. The physician diagnoses intestinal perforation and orders exploratory laparotomy; the nurse never attempts to palpate deeply or manipulate an acute rigid abdomen.
- **Priority Trap**: In a client with suspected typhoid fever who suddenly develops severe right lower abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen, the nurse's priority action is to place the client on NPO and notify the physician immediately (suspected bowel perforation), rather than offering pain medication or warm compresses.

## References
1. Maglaya, A. S., Nursing Practice in the Community, 5th Edition, Chapter 10.
2. Department of Health (DOH) Philippines, Philippine Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (PIDSR) Guidelines.
3. World Health Organization (WHO), Typhoid Fact Sheet and Communicable Disease Guidelines.
4. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Clinical Guidance for Typhoid Fever. https://www.cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html
5. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Clinical Overview of Typhoid Fever. https://www.cdc.gov/typhoid-fever/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html

## Check against your textbook
UNVERIFIED: Specific local antibiotic resistance patterns and exact regional DOH treatment protocols should be verified against the current DOH guidelines.
UNVERIFIED: the Maglaya textbook citation was not checked against the book; relative bradycardia, the step-ladder fever and rose-spot percentage come from review handouts, not from the CDC pages fetched.

title: Bacillary Dysentery (Shigellosis)
body:
## What it is
Shigellosis (bacillary dysentery, "bloody flux") is an acute infection of the large intestine caused by *Shigella* bacteria. It causes fever, cramping belly pain, tenesmus (the urge to pass stool even when the bowel is empty) and small, frequent stools with blood and mucus. It spreads very easily because only a tiny number of germs are needed to cause illness. Children, crowded households and evacuation centers are the usual setting.

## Causative agent
- Organism: *Shigella* species (*S. dysenteriae*, *S. flexneri*, *S. boydii*, *S. sonnei*), gram-negative rods. *S. dysenteriae* can make Shiga toxin and is linked to hemolytic-uremic syndrome (CDC).
- Transmission: fecal-oral. Swallowing something that touched the stool of an infected person: contaminated food, water, hands, objects, flies, and person-to-person contact (including sexual contact).
- Incubation period: CDC gives 1 to 2 days, with illness lasting about 7 days. Your handout gives 12-96 hours (up to a week); both overlap.
- Period of communicability: the handout says until the stool no longer contains the organism. CDC fetched pages do not state the infectious period; treat the duration as UNVERIFIED.
- Reservoir: humans. Flies and contaminated hands move the germ from stool to food.

## Main problem
The germ invades the lining of the colon, causing inflammation, tiny ulcers, mucus and blood in the stool. Cramping and tenesmus come from the inflamed rectum. Stools are small in volume, so severe dehydration is less common than in cholera, but it can still happen, especially in children and the elderly.

## Initial manifestations
- Fever, malaise, headache.
- Colicky lower abdominal pain and nausea or vomiting.
- Diarrhea that begins watery, then becomes bloody and mucoid.
- Tenesmus.

## Other manifestations
- Anorexia, weakness, dehydration.
- Seizures can occur occasionally in young children with high fever (CDC).
- Complications (CDC): post-infectious arthritis (about 2% with *S. flexneri*, in predisposed people), rare bloodstream infection in people with weak immunity, and hemolytic-uremic syndrome with Shiga-toxin-producing strains.
- Rectal prolapse can follow repeated straining (UNVERIFIED in fetched pages).

## Laboratory and diagnostic data
- Stool culture or a culture-independent test; a positive rapid test should be confirmed by culture, and susceptibility testing is done if an antibiotic will be used (CDC).
- Fresh stool microscopy: mucus, red and white blood cells (handout).
- Handout also lists immunofluorescence and sigmoidoscopy (shallow ulcers).
- Follow-up cultures may be needed if diarrhea lasts more than 3 days (CDC).

## Medical management
- The physician confirms the diagnosis with stool tests and decides whether treatment is needed, because many cases are mild and self-limited (CDC).
- The physician orders fluid replacement (oral or intravenous) according to dehydration.
- The physician orders an antibiotic for severe cases, chosen by susceptibility. CDC lists fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin, azithromycin and third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or ampicillin only if susceptibility is documented.
- The physician avoids antimotility drugs: CDC clinical care advises avoiding loperamide and diphenoxylate-atropine in shigellosis.
- The physician may order a low-residue diet as tolerated (handout).

## Pharmacologic care
- **Antibiotics** (prototype names: ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, ceftriaxone; per CDC). They shorten illness and reduce shedding in severe cases. Before: ask about allergies, pregnancy, age and kidney problems; check the culture and susceptibility report. During: give on schedule; for IV ceftriaxone, check the IV site. After: watch for diarrhea that worsens, rash or tendon pain. Adverse effects: nausea, rash; fluoroquinolones may cause tendon or joint problems (UNVERIFIED in fetched pages). Hold and report: hives, difficulty breathing, severe new diarrhea. Teaching: complete the course. Dose per physician order.
- **Oral rehydration salts and IV fluids**: replace water and salts. Give per physician order and ORS packet label; record intake and output.
- **Antimotility agents (loperamide, diphenoxylate-atropine)**: DO NOT give; the nurse should question any such order, because slowing the gut keeps the germ and toxin inside (CDC).
- **Antipyretic** for fever (for example paracetamol): dose per physician order.

## Nursing diagnoses
1. Deficient fluid volume related to diarrhea and vomiting as evidenced by dry mucosa, poor skin turgor and decreased urine output (priority).
2. Acute pain related to intestinal inflammation as evidenced by cramping and tenesmus.
3. Diarrhea related to bacterial invasion of the colon as evidenced by frequent bloody mucoid stools.
4. Risk for impaired skin integrity related to frequent stools.
5. Risk for infection transmission related to fecal contamination.

## Independent nursing interventions
1. Assess vital signs, hydration status and level of consciousness - detect dehydration or shock early.
2. Record intake, output, stool number, color and blood or mucus - shows severity and response.
3. Encourage oral fluids and small frequent feedings; offer low-residue food as tolerated - replaces loss and rests the bowel.
4. Apply enteric precautions: handwashing with soap, gloves for stool, dedicated toilet or commode - limits spread.
5. Dispose of stool and soiled linen safely and disinfect surfaces; control flies - removes the source.
6. Give perianal skin care and keep the area clean and dry - frequent bloody stools irritate skin.
7. Provide rest and comfort measures (warm position, privacy) for cramping and tenesmus - reduces distress.
8. Take a food, water and contact history, and identify other household members with symptoms - finds the source.
9. Teach handwashing after toilet and before eating, safe water and food, and not preparing food for others while ill - interrupts transmission.
10. Report to the barangay or municipal health office - controls spread to the community.

## Collaborative nursing interventions
1. As ordered: give the antibiotic - check allergies and stool susceptibility result first, give on time, and report rash or worsening diarrhea.
2. As ordered: start IV fluid for moderate-to-severe dehydration - verify the fluid and rate, monitor lungs and urine output, and report breathlessness.
3. As ordered: give ORS - check the patient can drink, give small sips, and report persistent vomiting.
4. As ordered: collect stool for culture and microscopy - use a clean container, label it and send promptly.
5. As ordered: give antipyretic for fever - check temperature before and after.
6. If an antidiarrheal is ordered: hold it and clarify with the physician - it is contraindicated in dysentery.

## Philippine context
- Shigellosis is a food- and waterborne disease handled within the DOH food and waterborne diseases surveillance work; UNVERIFIED: I could not confirm a specific Philippine program name or law number from a fetched page.
- Local risk setting: crowded evacuation centers, unsafe water, flies and open defecation.
- Local advice: handwashing with soap, boil water, sanitary toilets, cover food (control of flies).
- Filipino term: *dumi na may dugo* (bloody stool) prompts early consult.

## Exam traps
- **Antidiarrheals are contraindicated** - they hold the organism in and prolong fever. The right nursing response to such an order is to question it.
- **Nurse vs doctor:** Choosing the antibiotic is medical; the nurse independently records stools, rehydrates orally, applies enteric precautions and teaches handwashing.
- **Priority:** For a dehydrated child with bloody diarrhea, assess circulation and hydration before specimen collection or teaching.
- Bloody mucoid stool with tenesmus points to shigellosis; rice-water stool without cramps points to cholera.

## Quick memory aids
- **Shigella = Sharp cramps + Straining (tenesmus) + Stool with blood**.
- "Slow the gut, keep the bug" - why antimotility drugs are wrong.
- Small stools, big strain: dysentery. Big stools, big loss: cholera.

## References
1. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical Overview of Shigellosis. https://www.cdc.gov/shigella/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html
2. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Shigella Infection. https://www.cdc.gov/shigella/about/index.html
3. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical Care of Shigellosis. https://www.cdc.gov/shigella/hcp/clinical-care/index.html

## Check against your textbook
UNVERIFIED: the handout's incubation (12-96 hours) and period of communicability (until stool is free of the organism) were not stated on the CDC pages I fetched; CDC gives 1-2 days incubation.
UNVERIFIED: complete antibiotic dosing and local resistance patterns; check with your textbook and current DOH guidance.
See also [[Amoebiasis]], [[Cholera]], [[Typhoid Fever]].

title: Amoebiasis
body:
## What it is
Amoebiasis (amebiasis) is an infection of the large intestine by the protozoan *Entamoeba histolytica*. Many people carry it without symptoms (CDC says only about 10-20% of infected people become ill). When it does cause disease, it ranges from mild diarrhea to amoebic dysentery with bloody stool and fever. In a few patients the parasite travels through the blood to the liver, forming an abscess, or rarely to the lungs or brain.

## Causative agent
- Organism: *Entamoeba histolytica*, a protozoan with two forms. The **cyst** is the infective, hardy form that survives outside the body; the **trophozoite** is the active, invasive form that lives in the colon and dies quickly outside the body. A harmless look-alike, *E. dispar*, exists and needs special tests to tell apart (CDC).
- Transmission: fecal-oral. Swallowing cysts from contaminated water or food, unwashed hands or objects touched by infected stool; flies can carry cysts to food; fertilizer made from human waste can also spread it (MedlinePlus). Person-to-person spread is possible but low with good hygiene.
- Incubation period: usually 2 to 4 weeks, sometimes longer (CDC); the handout agrees.
- Period of communicability: as long as cysts are passed in the stool, which may be for years if untreated (handout: while cysts are in stool).
- Reservoir: humans, especially symptom-free carriers. Poor sanitation, unsafe water and food handlers who are carriers keep it going.

## Main problem
Trophozoites attack the wall of the colon, producing flask-shaped ulcers, bloody mucoid stool and, if they reach the portal circulation, abscesses in the liver. The harmful effects are tissue destruction in the bowel and possible spread to the liver, lungs and brain.

## Initial manifestations
- Mild cases: cramps, diarrhea, gas, fatigue and weight loss; many people have no symptoms at all (MedlinePlus).
- Acute amoebic dysentery: stomach pain, bloody mucoid stool and fever (CDC).
- Handout adds: diarrhea alternating with constipation, foul watery stool streaked with blood and mucus, lower abdominal gas and right iliac tenderness.

## Other manifestations
- Chronic: weeks of diarrhea alternating with constipation, weight loss, weakness and bloody mucoid stools (handout).
- Complications: amoebic liver abscess (right upper quadrant pain, fever); less often spread to lungs and brain (CDC). Severe colitis can lead to perforation (UNVERIFIED in fetched pages).
- Dehydration from diarrhea.

## Laboratory and diagnostic data
- Stool examination, often repeated on different days because the parasite is not always present (CDC, MedlinePlus). Handout: stool exam for cysts, and trophozoites in fresh, warm specimens.
- Specialized tests can distinguish *E. histolytica* from harmless *E. dispar*; liver abscess fluid can also be tested (CDC).
- MedlinePlus lists blood tests and sigmoidoscopy (ulcers seen on the colon wall); handout notes leukocytosis.
- Specimen care: no oil-based preparations or barium for about 48 hours beforehand, choose the portion with blood and mucus, label, send immediately and keep warm so trophozoites stay alive (handout; the 48-hour detail is UNVERIFIED in fetched pages).

## Medical management
- The physician confirms the diagnosis by stool tests and decides whether the patient is symptomatic or only a carrier.
- The physician orders antibiotic treatment. CDC states that people who are not sick usually take one antibiotic, while sick people usually take a second one after finishing the first.
- The physician avoids antidiarrheal drugs, which are generally avoided because they can worsen the condition (MedlinePlus).
- The physician orders fluid replacement for dehydration, imaging if a liver abscess is suspected, and surgery or drainage only for complications.

## Pharmacologic care
- **Nitroimidazole antiprotozoals** (prototype: metronidazole; tinidazole is another). They kill trophozoites in the bowel wall and in the liver. Before: ask about alcohol use, pregnancy and past reactions. During: give with or after food to reduce nausea. After: watch for dizziness, metallic taste, nausea, dark urine or numbness. Hold and report: seizure, numbness or tingling, severe vomiting, rash. Teaching: **avoid alcohol** during and shortly after treatment (disulfiram-like reaction; UNVERIFIED in fetched pages), finish the course. Dose per physician order. The handout's metronidazole dose (800 mg TID x 5 days) is NOT verified by any page I fetched; do not memorize it.
- **Luminal amoebicides** (for example paromomycin) clear cysts left in the bowel after the first drug (CDC describes a second antibiotic after the first; the generic name paromomycin is UNVERIFIED in fetched pages). Before: check allergies and kidney function. After: monitor stool pattern. Dose per physician order.
- The handout also lists tetracycline, ampicillin, streptomycin and chloramphenicol; current practice differs, so rely on the physician's order.
- **ORS or IV fluids** for dehydration: per physician order.

## Nursing diagnoses
1. Diarrhea related to colonic invasion by *E. histolytica* as evidenced by frequent bloody mucoid stools (priority).
2. Deficient fluid volume related to diarrhea as evidenced by thirst, dry mucosa and poor skin turgor.
3. Acute pain related to intestinal inflammation as evidenced by cramping and right iliac tenderness.
4. Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements related to anorexia and malabsorption as evidenced by weight loss.
5. Deficient knowledge regarding sanitation and food hygiene as evidenced by unsafe water and excreta practices.

## Independent nursing interventions
1. Assess vital signs, hydration and abdominal pain; note any right upper quadrant pain or fever - may signal liver abscess.
2. Apply enteric precautions: handwashing, gloves with stool, separate toilet or commode - prevents cyst spread.
3. Collect the stool correctly (warm container, portion with blood and mucus, labeled, sent immediately; no oil preparations beforehand) - live trophozoites die when the stool cools.
4. Record intake, output, stool number and character - shows severity and response.
5. Encourage oral fluids and a bland, low-residue diet as tolerated; keep the patient warm - replaces loss and reduces cramping.
6. Provide perianal skin care and rest - frequent stools break down skin.
7. Teach hand washing with soap before eating and after toilet, boiling or chlorinating water, and washing fruit and vegetables - cuts fecal-oral spread.
8. Teach food handlers and carriers that they must not prepare food for others until cleared - carriers are an important reservoir.
9. Promote environmental sanitation: sanitary toilet, fly control, protected food and water - removes the source.
10. Refer household members for stool examination and report to the health office - finds other carriers.

## Collaborative nursing interventions
1. As ordered: give metronidazole or the prescribed antiprotozoal - check allergies and alcohol use first, give with food, and hold and report seizures, numbness or severe vomiting.
2. As ordered: give the second (luminal) drug after the first course - confirm the sequence with the order, and monitor stool.
3. As ordered: start IV fluid or give ORS for dehydration - verify the rate, monitor urine output, and report breathlessness.
4. As ordered: send repeat stool specimens - label them with the time and send immediately.
5. As ordered: prepare the patient for sigmoidoscopy or imaging - explain the procedure and check for bleeding or perforation signs afterward.
6. As ordered: give analgesic or antipyretic - check temperature and pain level before and after.

## Philippine context
- Amoebiasis is a common waterborne and foodborne infection under the DOH food- and waterborne disease work; UNVERIFIED: I did not fetch a Philippine page confirming program names or numbers.
- Local settings: areas without safe water or toilets, floods, and food bought from street vendors.
- Local advice: boil water at least 1 minute (CDC), wash hands, use sanitary toilets, control flies, and cook food well.
- Filipino terms: *disenterya*, *amoeba*.

## Exam traps
- **Specimen trap:** the stool must be fresh and warm for trophozoites; do not refrigerate it, and no oil preparations beforehand.
- **Nurse action vs doctor action:** prescribing metronidazole and ordering imaging are medical; the nurse independently collects the specimen correctly, applies enteric precautions and teaches handwashing.
- **Priority trap:** a patient with bloody diarrhea who becomes drowsy with a weak pulse needs circulation assessed and fluids first, not a stool specimen.
- Antidiarrheals are avoided in amoebic dysentery.
- Cyst = infective and tough; trophozoite = invasive but fragile.

## Quick memory aids
- **Cyst = Carries it (infective); Trophozoite = Tears the bowel (invasive).**
- "Warm and quick": warm stool, sent quickly.
- Think "alternating diarrhea and constipation, liver abscess" for amoebiasis.

## References
1. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Amebiasis. https://www.cdc.gov/amebiasis/about/index.html
2. MedlinePlus. Amebiasis. https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000298.htm

## Check against your textbook
The handout's metronidazole dose (800 mg TID x 5 days) should be verified; do not memorize it without checking.
UNVERIFIED: the paromomycin name, the alcohol warning and the 48-hour "no oil" rule are not stated on the pages I fetched.
UNVERIFIED: only two sources were fetched for this note (CDC, MedlinePlus); the NCBI StatPearls page was blocked.
See also [[Bacillary Dysentery (Shigellosis)]], [[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]], [[Trichomoniasis]].

title: Paragonimiasis (Lung Fluke)
body:
## What it is
Paragonimiasis (lung fluke disease) is a foodborne parasitic infection caused by flukes of the genus *Paragonimus*. The adult worms settle in the lungs and cause a long-lasting cough with blood-streaked sputum and chest pain. The disease is easy to mistake for tuberculosis, which is why it is a favorite exam topic.

## Causative agent
- Organism: *Paragonimus westermani* (the oriental lung fluke) is the most common human species (CDC); your handout also lists *P. siamensis*. More than 30 *Paragonimus* species infect animals and humans.
- Transmission: eating raw, undercooked or pickled freshwater crabs or crayfish that carry the infective larvae (metacercariae). Drinking contaminated water or swimming does not spread it (WHO). Handout adds using the meat or juice of infected animals.
- Life cycle and intermediate hosts: eggs leave the body in sputum or stool and reach water. The first intermediate host is a freshwater **snail**; the second is a freshwater **crab or crayfish**, where the larvae encyst. After a person eats the larvae, they escape in the duodenum, travel through the intestinal wall, the abdominal cavity and the diaphragm, and settle in the lungs as adults (CDC).
- Incubation period: eggs appear in 65 to 90 days after infection (CDC), so symptoms and egg-positive sputum may take 2-3 months to appear; infection can last up to 20 years.
- Period of communicability: not directly spread from person to person. An infected person keeps shedding eggs (which need snails and crabs to complete the cycle), so the risk is through the environment and food.
- Reservoir: humans and animals, including pigs, dogs and cats (CDC; handout lists cats, dogs, rats and pigs). Freshwater crabs are the key food source in the Philippines. UNVERIFIED: specific endemic provinces were not confirmed from a fetched page.

## Main problem
Adult flukes living in lung tissue provoke inflammation and cysts that connect to the airways, producing cough, bloody sputum and chest pain. The disease looks like tuberculosis on symptoms and chest imaging. If the worms reach the brain, they cause headaches, seizures and nerve damage.

## Initial manifestations
- Acute phase: diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, cough, hives, and enlarged liver and spleen, with high eosinophil counts (CDC).
- Chronic phase: cough that does not go away, rust-colored or blood-streaked sputum, and chest pain (CDC; WHO).

## Other manifestations
- Recurring hemoptysis, shortness of breath, abnormal chest X-ray (CDC; WHO).
- Cerebral paragonimiasis: headaches, seizures and neurologic damage (WHO).
- Worms may settle in other organs and cause more severe disease (CDC).
- The illness is **TB-like but does not respond to anti-TB drugs** (handout; WHO says it closely resembles TB and is often misdiagnosed).

## Laboratory and diagnostic data
- Microscopy of sputum or stool for eggs; concentration techniques may be needed in light infections (CDC).
- Antibody (serologic) tests - complement fixation, enzyme immunoassay, immunoblot - are often more useful because eggs are hard to find (CDC).
- Biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and the species if a fluke is recovered (CDC).
- Chest X-ray changes mimic TB; ask for sputum examination for eggs when TB tests are negative (WHO).

## Medical management
- The physician rules out tuberculosis and confirms paragonimiasis by sputum, stool or antibody tests.
- The physician orders an antiparasitic drug. WHO states triclabendazole is first-line, with praziquantel as an alternative when triclabendazole is unavailable. Your handout names praziquantel.
- The physician arranges follow-up testing to confirm cure (WHO) and further workup or treatment if the brain is involved.
- The physician (with public health officers) coordinates community control.

## Pharmacologic care
- **Anthelmintic (antiparasitic) drugs**: triclabendazole (WHO first-line) and praziquantel (alternative). They kill the adult flukes. Before: ask about allergies, pregnancy and other drugs, and confirm the diagnosis with the physician. During: give as ordered, with food if directed. After: watch for dizziness, headache, nausea, abdominal discomfort or rash. Hold and report: severe headache, seizure, difficulty breathing, rash. Teaching: finish the course, attend follow-up sputum checks, and do not eat raw crab again. Dose per physician order; no dose is stated on the pages I fetched.
- **Analgesic or cough relief**: only as ordered; do not suppress a cough that is needed to clear secretions without an order.
- **Anticonvulsants** only if the physician orders them for cerebral paragonimiasis.

## Nursing diagnoses
1. Ineffective airway clearance related to chronic cough and bloody sputum as evidenced by cough and hemoptysis (priority).
2. Impaired gas exchange related to lung tissue involvement as evidenced by chest pain and shortness of breath.
3. Acute pain related to inflammation of the chest as evidenced by chest and back pain.
4. Deficient knowledge regarding raw crab consumption as evidenced by a history of eating uncooked crustaceans.
5. Risk for injury related to seizures in brain involvement.

## Independent nursing interventions
1. Assess airway, breathing and oxygenation (respiratory rate, breath sounds, color, amount of blood in sputum) - airway comes first.
2. Position the patient in semi-Fowler's to improve breathing - eases lung expansion.
3. Teach effective coughing and deep breathing, and give oral care after coughing - helps clear secretions and comfort.
4. Take a careful diet and travel history, including raw, undercooked or pickled crab or crayfish - the history points to the diagnosis and the source.
5. Record the sputum amount and color; label and send sputum specimens correctly - provides evidence for diagnosis.
6. Provide rest, comfort and nutrition; encourage oral fluids - supports recovery.
7. Observe for neurologic signs (headache, seizure) and keep the side rails padded if there are any - protects from injury.
8. Teach the family to cook crabs and crayfish thoroughly and avoid raw or pickled preparations - breaks the transmission.
9. Teach safe sputum disposal and general hygiene - reduces egg contamination of water.
10. Refer the household and neighbors who ate the same food for screening, and report to the health office - finds other cases.

## Collaborative nursing interventions
1. As ordered: give the anthelmintic (triclabendazole or praziquantel) - check allergies first, give as directed, and hold and report rash, seizure or severe headache.
2. As ordered: collect sputum for eggs on several days - use a clean container, label it and send promptly.
3. As ordered: prepare the patient for a chest X-ray, CT or other imaging - explain the procedure and check for pregnancy where applicable.
4. As ordered: give oxygen if hypoxic - monitor oxygen saturation and respiratory rate.
5. As ordered: give anticonvulsants if prescribed - monitor for sedation and seizure control.
6. As ordered: arrange follow-up sputum or antibody tests to confirm cure - explain the schedule to the patient.

## Philippine context
- Paragonimiasis is a food-borne parasitic disease linked to eating raw freshwater crabs. WHO reports that the Philippines has run integrated surveillance for paragonimiasis and TB, because the diseases are confused.
- Dietary habits (raw, undercooked or pickled crabs) keep transmission going in endemic communities. UNVERIFIED: the specific endemic provinces (for example Sorsogon, Leyte, Mindanao areas appeared in a search summary only) were not confirmed from a fetched page.
- Teaching point: cook freshwater crabs and crayfish thoroughly; marinating or pickling alone does not make them safe (CDC lists pickled crab as a route).
- UNVERIFIED: a named DOH national program for paragonimiasis could not be verified.

## Exam traps
- **TB look-alike:** chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum, no improvement on anti-TB drugs, and a history of eating raw crab = paragonimiasis.
- **Nurse vs doctor:** choosing triclabendazole or praziquantel is medical; the nurse independently takes the diet history, teaches thorough cooking and collects sputum properly.
- **Snail caution:** the snail is the first intermediate host, but infection in people happens by eating crab or crayfish, not by touching snails or water (contrast with schistosomiasis).
- **Priority:** for hemoptysis with breathing difficulty, assess airway and breathing first.

## Quick memory aids
- **Crab, Cough, Coughing blood** - "3 Cs" of paragonimiasis.
- TB mimic that does not respond to TB drugs.
- Cook the crab through; do not just marinate it.

## References
1. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. DPDx Paragonimiasis. https://www.cdc.gov/dpdx/paragonimiasis/index.html
2. World Health Organization. Neglected tropical diseases: Paragonimiasis. https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/neglected-tropical-diseases-paragonimiasis

## Check against your textbook
The handout calls praziquantel "Billtrizide" and lists anti-mollusk campaigns, which belong more to schistosomiasis; confirm control measures.
UNVERIFIED: the "Billtrizide" brand name and the handout's snail-control campaigns were not found on the pages I fetched.
UNVERIFIED: the Philippine endemic provinces, DOH program and any law number.
See also [[Tuberculosis: Features and Diagnosis]], [[Schistosomiasis]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]].

title: Mumps
body:
## What it is
Mumps (*beke* in Filipino) is an acute viral infection that mainly causes painful swelling of the parotid (salivary) glands in front of and below the ears, on one or both sides. It also affects the testes, ovaries, pancreas and brain coverings in some patients. It is prevented by the MMR vaccine. See [[Measles (Rubeola)]] and [[German Measles (Rubella)]] for the other two diseases in the MMR group.

## Causative agent
- Organism: mumps virus, a paramyxovirus (CDC).
- Transmission: close contact; spread by droplets of saliva and respiratory secretions and by articles soiled with nose and throat secretions (handout).
- Incubation period: average 16-18 days, range 12-25 days (CDC); CDC's public page says symptoms start 2-4 weeks after infection.
- Period of communicability: **2 days before to 5 days after parotitis begins** (CDC). Virus has been found in saliva from 7 days before to 9 days after onset, and in urine and semen for up to 14 days.
- Reservoir: humans only. Many cases today occur in fully vaccinated people in crowded settings such as schools and dormitories, usually milder.

## Main problem
The virus infects the salivary glands and may spread to other organs. The main problems are pain with chewing and swallowing, fever, risk of complications (inflammation of the testes, brain coverings or brain, pancreas, deafness), and spread in closed communities.

## Initial manifestations
- Fever, headache, muscle aches, tiredness, loss of appetite, earache (handout).
- Tender swelling of the parotid gland between the earlobe and the angle of the jaw, one side or both; swelling peaks in 1-3 days and subsides over about a week (CDC).
- Pain on chewing or swallowing, especially sour foods.

## Other manifestations
- Submandibular and sublingual glands may also swell.
- Orchitis (painful swollen testis) in post-pubertal males can threaten fertility (handout); oophoritis, mastitis in females (handout).
- Complications listed by CDC: encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, viral pneumonia, hemorrhagic conditions; historically permanent deafness. The handout adds meningoencephalitis, pancreatitis, myocarditis, nephritis.
- Most patients recover fully within about 2 weeks.

## Laboratory and diagnostic data
- RT-PCR and viral culture confirm infection; buccal swabs are most commonly used (CDC).
- IgM serology can help but interpretation depends on vaccination status and timing; a negative result does not rule out mumps (CDC).
- The handout also lists serum amylase (raised in parotitis), complement fixation and hemagglutination inhibition.

## Medical management
- The physician diagnoses from the swelling and exposure history and may order PCR to confirm.
- There is no specific antiviral treatment (MedlinePlus); the physician orders supportive care.
- The physician evaluates and treats complications (testicular pain, severe headache or stiff neck, abdominal pain).
- The physician advises isolation until 5 days after parotitis onset and reports the case.

## Pharmacologic care
- **Analgesic-antipyretics** (prototype: paracetamol/acetaminophen; ibuprofen may be ordered for adults). They relieve pain and lower fever. Dose per physician order. Before: check temperature, pain score and liver history. During: give on schedule. After: reassess pain and fever. Hold and report: persistent high fever, severe headache or neck stiffness, testicular swelling. Teach: do not exceed the daily limit; avoid aspirin in children (Reye syndrome).
- **Anti-inflammatory or steroid drugs** for orchitis, only if the physician orders. Dose per physician order. Before: check for infection and stomach problems. During: give with food. After: watch for stomach pain and blood sugar changes. Teach: do not stop abruptly if on a longer course.
- **MMR vaccine** (live attenuated; prevention). CDC recommends 2 doses for children; a third dose may be advised for people at higher risk in an outbreak. Dose per physician or program order. Before: screen for pregnancy, immunosuppression and allergy. After: watch for fever, mild rash, swollen glands and allergic reaction. Teach: complete the series.

## Nursing diagnoses
1. Acute pain (priority) related to inflammation and swelling of the parotid gland, as evidenced by pain on chewing and swallowing and facial tenderness.
2. Hyperthermia related to viral infection, as evidenced by fever.
3. Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements related to painful chewing, as evidenced by poor intake.
4. Risk for infection transmission related to viral shedding in saliva.
5. Risk for complications (orchitis, meningitis) related to systemic spread of the virus.

## Independent nursing interventions
1. Apply droplet precautions in a single room per policy until 5 days after parotitis onset - protects others.
2. Assess pain, temperature, swelling and signs of complications (stiff neck, severe headache, testicular pain, abdominal pain) every shift - early detection.
3. Apply warm or cold compresses to the swollen glands as comfortable (handout) - eases pain.
4. Give a soft, bland diet and avoid acid foods and juices (handout) - acid stimulates saliva flow and increases pain.
5. Encourage extra fluids and small, frequent feedings - prevents dehydration and malnutrition.
6. Provide oral care with warm salt-water gargles (handout) - cleanliness and comfort.
7. Support the scrotum and provide bed rest if testicular pain or swelling occurs, and report it - comfort and protection.
8. Keep the patient at home away from school or work until 5 days after swelling begins - community protection.
9. Teach hand hygiene, no sharing of cups and utensils, and covering coughs - limits spread.
10. Report the case and trace unvaccinated contacts - surveillance.

## Collaborative nursing interventions
1. As ordered: give analgesics and antipyretics; check pain score, temperature and last dose, and report pain not relieved or persistent fever.
2. As ordered: give anti-inflammatory drugs or apply cold packs for orchitis; check for stomach upset and watch for infection, and report worsening swelling.
3. As ordered: give IV fluids if the patient cannot drink; check intake and output, monitor the rate, and report poor urine output.
4. As ordered: collect swab, urine or blood for mumps tests; check labeling and timing and report results.
5. As ordered: give MMR vaccine to susceptible contacts; check pregnancy, immune status and allergy first, observe afterward, and report reactions.

## Philippine context
- Mumps is called *beke* in Filipino (from the project brief; not confirmed by a fetched page).
- MMR is part of the national immunization effort (DOH routine MMR at 9-12 months, GMA Mar 2025); see [[Expanded Program on Immunization]]. I did not verify whether mumps-specific doses are included in your school notes.
- Mumps is a notifiable disease; RA 11332 (2019) requires public and private entities to report notifiable diseases; check the current DOH list.
- Local exam angle: school or dormitory outbreak and a teenage boy with testicular pain.

## Exam traps
- Nurse vs doctor: the nurse relieves pain and isolates; the physician orders analgesics, steroids and the vaccine.
- Priority trap: assess for meningitis and orchitis (stiff neck, severe headache, testicular pain) before diet teaching.
- Diet trap: sour foods and juices hurt; give bland, soft food.
- Communicability trap: contagious before the swelling shows, so isolation covers the 5 days after onset.
- Swelling is below and in front of the ear, not under the tongue.

## Quick memory aids
- "Mumps = Munch pain": it hurts to chew; sour makes it worse.
- Complication list "MOP": Meningitis, Orchitis, Pancreatitis.
- MMR protects the "M, M, R".

## References
1. CDC. Mumps clinical overview for clinicians: https://www.cdc.gov/mumps/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html
2. CDC. About mumps: https://www.cdc.gov/mumps/about/index.html
3. MedlinePlus. Mumps: https://medlineplus.gov/mumps.html

## Check against your textbook
UNVERIFIED: no handout section; confirm serum amylase, bland diet advice, orchitis details and the notifiable status in your textbook.

title: Botulism
body:
## What it is
Botulism is a rare but life-threatening illness caused by a nerve toxin made by *Clostridium botulinum* (and sometimes related bacteria). The toxin blocks the release of the chemical that makes muscles contract, producing a **descending flaccid paralysis** that starts in the eyes and face and can reach the breathing muscles. It is a medical emergency. Forms: foodborne, wound, infant, and others (iatrogenic, adult intestinal toxemia, and inhalation).

## Causative agent
- Organism: *Clostridium botulinum*, a gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobe found in soil and water. Types A, B, E and rarely F cause human disease (WHO). Its spores are heat-resistant; the toxin forms where oxygen is absent.
- Transmission: **foodborne** - eating food that already contains the toxin, such as improperly home-canned, preserved or fermented food, and (per the handout) cured meats and smoked fish. **Infant** - spores grow in the gut of infants, mainly under 6 months, and honey has been linked. **Wound** - spores enter an open wound, linked to injected drugs such as black tar heroin. Person-to-person spread does not occur.
- Incubation period: WHO gives foodborne symptoms usually within 12 to 36 hours, with a range of 4 hours to 8 days; wound botulism can take up to 2 weeks. Your handout's 12-72 hours is a broader range.
- Period of communicability: not spread from person to person. The danger is the food or wound source and anyone else who ate the same food.
- Reservoir: soil and water; spores are widespread. UNVERIFIED: no Philippine-specific reservoir page was found.

## Main problem
The toxin binds to nerve endings and prevents acetylcholine release. Muscles cannot contract, so weakness progresses downward: eyes, face, throat, then limbs and the diaphragm. Respiratory failure is the major threat to life. There is no fever and the patient stays alert (WHO).

## Initial manifestations
- Double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids (ptosis).
- Dry mouth, slurred speech, trouble swallowing.
- Fatigue, weakness and dizziness.
- Early nausea, vomiting or diarrhea in foodborne cases, later constipation (handout; WHO notes GI symptoms may occur).

## Other manifestations
- Descending weakness of the neck, arms, trunk and legs; reduced reflexes (handout).
- Respiratory muscle weakness leading to shortness of breath and respiratory failure.
- Infants: constipation, poor feeding, weak cry, floppy head control (WHO).
- No fever and clear thinking (WHO), which helps separate it from infections.

## Laboratory and diagnostic data
- Diagnosis is mainly clinical; confirmation is by finding the toxin in serum, stool or food, or by culture of the bacterium (WHO). The handout adds the mouse test as the most direct method (UNVERIFIED in fetched pages) and EMG.
- It is easily mistaken for stroke, Guillain-Barre syndrome or myasthenia gravis, so these are ruled out (WHO).
- Never delay treatment while waiting for lab confirmation (WHO states antitoxin should be given as soon as possible).

## Medical management
- The physician makes the clinical diagnosis and orders the botulinum antitoxin as soon as possible; early antitoxin reduces mortality (WHO).
- The physician decides on mechanical ventilation. Severe cases need intensive supportive care, and ventilation may last weeks to months (WHO).
- The physician reports the case at once to the health authorities so others who ate the same food can be found.
- Antibiotics are not needed except for wound botulism (WHO); wound cleaning or surgery is done for infected wounds (MedlinePlus).
- The physician may order gut decontamination in selected foodborne cases (the handout mentions purging the GI tract; this is UNVERIFIED in fetched pages and the handout's suggestion to induce vomiting in infants is not standard).

## Pharmacologic care
- **Botulinum antitoxin (antivenom-type biologic)**: it neutralizes toxin that is circulating but cannot undo paralysis already established, so early use matters. The nurse's role: Before - confirm the physician's order, ask about allergies, previous equine (horse) serum reactions and asthma, and have emergency drugs and airway equipment ready; do any sensitivity test only as ordered by the physician. During - give by the ordered route and rate, stay with the patient, and monitor vital signs and for hives, wheezing, hypotension or fever. After - continue frequent neurologic and respiratory checks, because paralysis improves slowly as new nerve endings grow. Hold and report: rash, wheezing, drop in blood pressure or any breathing change. Teaching: explain what the drug does and does not do, and that recovery is slow. No dose is given here; dose per physician order or protocol.
- **Antibiotics** only for wound botulism (WHO): dose per physician order. Some antibiotics may worsen weakness; clarify with the physician (UNVERIFIED in fetched pages).
- **Supportive care**: oxygen and mechanical ventilation, IV fluids and nutrition via tube as ordered.

## Nursing diagnoses
1. Ineffective breathing pattern related to respiratory muscle paralysis as evidenced by shallow respirations, dyspnea and falling oxygen saturation (priority).
2. Impaired swallowing related to cranial nerve paralysis as evidenced by difficulty swallowing and risk of aspiration.
3. Impaired physical mobility related to flaccid paralysis as evidenced by muscle weakness.
4. Risk for aspiration related to weakened swallowing and gag reflex.
5. Deficient knowledge regarding safe food preservation as evidenced by home canning or consumption of improperly preserved food.

## Independent nursing interventions
1. Assess airway, breathing and oxygenation continuously (respiratory rate, depth, vital capacity if measured, oxygen saturation) - respiratory failure is the main cause of death, so ABCs come first.
2. Keep intubation and suction equipment at the bedside and position the head of the bed up unless otherwise ordered - ready for rapid airway support.
3. Make the patient NPO if swallowing is weak and report - prevents aspiration.
4. Perform frequent neurologic checks (eyelids, speech, swallowing, grip strength, reflexes) - detects a descending progression early.
5. Prevent complications of immobility: reposition every 2 hours, skin care, passive range of motion - paralysis causes pressure sores and contractures.
6. Provide eye care and oral care; keep communication simple (the patient is alert but may be unable to speak) - comfort and dignity.
7. Take a food history, including home-canned, fermented or smoked foods and honey in infants, and identify others who ate the same food - the other exposed people may need urgent care.
8. Notify the physician and the health authorities right away - botulism is a reportable emergency.
9. Teach safe food handling: do not eat from bulging cans, boil home-canned foods before eating if the physician or health worker advises (the old note said 10 minutes; UNVERIFIED), and never feed honey to infants under 1 year (WHO).
10. Provide emotional support and explanation to the patient and family - recovery can take weeks to months.

## Collaborative nursing interventions
1. As ordered: give botulinum antitoxin - check allergy history and sensitivity instructions with the physician first, give as directed, and stop and report hives, wheezing or low blood pressure.
2. As ordered: assist with intubation and mechanical ventilation - prepare equipment, monitor ventilator settings and secretions, and report falling oxygen saturation.
3. As ordered: insert an NG tube and give tube feeding - check placement before each feeding and watch for residual or aspiration.
4. As ordered: collect serum, stool and food samples - use clean containers, label them and send immediately.
5. As ordered: give IV fluids, oxygen and antibiotics (wound botulism only) - monitor effects and report adverse reactions.
6. As ordered: prepare for transfer to an intensive care unit - hand over neurologic and respiratory findings.

## Philippine context
- Foodborne botulism is rare in the Philippines. A search of Philippine news and outbreak studies did not turn up a DOH report of a foodborne botulism outbreak; a published review of foodborne outbreaks (2005-2018) lists other causes such as *Salmonella* and *Vibrio parahaemolyticus* (search summary only; UNVERIFIED).
- Infant botulism is also a concern with contaminated products; an alert about a recalled infant formula was reported in November 2025 (search summary; UNVERIFIED).
- Exam angle: home-canned or preserved foods (for example fish, vegetables), honey for infants and drug-injection wounds.
- Botulism is a notifiable condition for health authorities; UNVERIFIED: specific Philippine law numbers or DOH program names were not confirmed from a fetched page.

## Exam traps
- **Descending** weakness (eyes and face first) is botulism; **ascending** weakness points to Guillain-Barre.
- **Priority trap:** airway and breathing come first - not the food history, the antitoxin or the specimen. Check respirations before everything else.
- **Nurse vs doctor:** ordering antitoxin and ventilation are medical actions; the nurse monitors respiratory function, keeps equipment ready, and gives the drug only as ordered after the allergy history.
- No fever and a clear sensorium are classic; infection and meningitis are not the picture.
- Honey is dangerous for infants under 1 year, not for older children and adults.

## Quick memory aids
- **Botulism = "Blurred vision, Drooping lids, Dry mouth, Dysphagia"** - the four Ds, then breathing fails.
- "Down it goes": paralysis descends from head to toes.
- No honey before the first birthday.

## References
1. World Health Organization. Botulism fact sheet. https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/botulism
2. MedlinePlus. Botulism. https://medlineplus.gov/botulism.html
3. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Botulism. https://www.cdc.gov/botulism/about/index.html

## Check against your textbook
Handout suggests inducing vomiting in infants; this is not standard. Confirm.
UNVERIFIED: the mouse test, the "boil home-canned food 10 minutes" rule and the antitoxin skin-test step were not stated on the pages I fetched.
UNVERIFIED: Philippine reporting law number and any DOH botulism program.
See also [[Tetanus (Lockjaw) Disease]], [[Anthrax]], [[Poliomyelitis]].

title: Schistosomiasis
body:
## What it is
Schistosomiasis ("snail fever", *bilharziasis*) is a disease caused by blood flukes that enter the body through the skin during contact with infested fresh water. In the Philippines the species is *Schistosoma japonicum*. The adult worms live in blood vessels of the bowel and liver, and it is the eggs, not the worms, that cause most of the damage: inflammation, scarring (fibrosis) of the liver and bowel, portal hypertension and, rarely, brain involvement.

## Causative agent
